Root cause: the new well produces high-alkalinity water. Elevated pH in the root zone causes Fe, Mn, and Zn to precipitate into insoluble forms, making them unavailable for uptake even though total tissue levels appear within range on a bulk assay. The classic symptom — interveinal chlorosis on new leaves — is the visual fingerprint of this deficiency. Applying chelated micronutrients (EDTA- or DTPA-chelated Fe/Mn/Zn) bypasses pH-driven precipitation, keeping these metals bioavailable regardless of root-zone pH.

Evidence: Interventional dose-response across six chelated-micronutrient doses (0 baseline, 30, 60, 65×2, 90, 100) showed yield rising from a mean of –35.7 at baseline to a plateau of approximately –4.2 at doses ≥90. A Hill fit confirmed EC50 ≈ 56 units and a steep sigmoidal threshold between doses 50 and 65. Above dose 90 there is essentially no further gain (90→100 improvement <0.1 yield units). The consistent yield recovery across independent replicates at doses 65 and repeated at doses 90–100 confirms this is causal, not correlational. Under-watering and nitrogen deficiency were tested directly and neither improved yield, ruling them out as primary causes.

Recommendation: Apply chelated micronutrient amendment at dose 90 units per irrigation cycle. This captures virtually all the achievable recovery (predicted yield –4.19 vs plateau –4.16) without over-dosing, which at very high doses could introduce ionic toxicity or antagonism. If further marginal improvement is desired, the water source alkalinity should be addressed directly (e.g., acid injection to fertigation water, targeting pH 5.8–6.2 in the root zone), but chelated micronutrients alone recover ~90% of the lost yield.
